content.text: {"paragraph_1": "The argument, taken in order, runs like this: the prerequisite chapter establishes from Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9-10) that Scripture itself reads the sun, moon, and stars as persons in a household, and then fills in the offices — the Father as the sun ('the LORD God is a sun,' Psalm 84:11), the Son as the moon that has no light of its own but faithfully returns the sun's ('a faithful witness in heaven,' Psalm 89:37, handed to Christ by name in Revelation 1:5), and the righteous as the stars who rule the night with Him (Daniel 12:3; Psalm 136:9). The 'relay of light' built on 1 Corinthians 11:3 and 11:7, with Paul's own 'glory of the sun... glory of the moon' vocabulary from 15:41, resolves the obvious objection that Malachi calls the Son the Sun of righteousness: these are relational offices, not fixed identities, so the moon can figure the Son toward the Father and the bride toward her Bridegroom. Pearls of Wisdom then argues the merchant of Matthew 13:45-46 is the Son, not the seeking sinner, because the adjacent parable's buyer is fixed by Jesus's own interpretation — the sower is the Son of man, the field is the world (13:37-38) — and the treasure is God's 'peculiar treasure' (Exodus 19:5); the pearl is therefore the bride He purchased, and the full moon is her portrait in the sky. As a traditional reader I found real substance here. The Christological reading of the merchant is not actually alien to tradition — Christ purchasing His church 'with his own blood' (Acts 20:28) and giving Himself for her (Ephesians 5:25) is our own doctrine, and the standard 'sell all to gain the kingdom' reading has always sat uneasily beside salvation by grace. The tracing of merchant, merchandise, finding, and pearl-price through Proverbs 3:14-15, 18:22, and 31:10-31 is genuinely striking, especially the woman who rises while it is yet night, whose lamp does not go out in the night, who gives the appointed portion (choq) to her household as the faithful and wise servant of Matthew 24:45 gives meat in due season, and whose husband 'praiseth' her with the verb halal that elsewhere means to shine. And Song of Solomon 6:9-10 naming the one woman above the daughters 'fair as the moon' does read like a signature on the portrait. Even the church-as-moon figure has patristic pedigree; the ancients spoke of the mysterium lunae, the church shining with borrowed light. Read together, the two chapters make a coherent and often scripturally anchored case that the pearl is the bride and the bride is pictured in lunar terms.", "paragraph_2": "The objections that remain are not merely that this is unfamiliar; several load-bearing joints are weaker than the prose admits. First, the whole chain hangs on 'restoring' pearls for peninim in Proverbs 3:15, 31:10, Job 28:18, and Lamentations 4:7 — but even the cited authority says only 'probably a pearl,' and Lamentations 4:7 ('more ruddy in body than peninim') is itself evidence that the word means something red, coral or rubies, which is why the KJV translators chose as they did; a red gem breaks the white-round-complete argument at its root, and the chapter re-reads that very verse as a blood moon rather than facing the lexical problem. Second, the 'Hebrew text' of Revelation, James, and Jude — a Cochin manuscript of about 1700 — is used to do heavy work: rewriting Revelation 12:1 from 'a crown of twelve stars' to 'from her head begins the cycle, the first of the twelve stars,' turning the angels of the seven churches into 'seven elders,' and supplying James's 'no exchange of light and darkness.' A seventeenth-century manuscript is almost certainly a translation from the Greek or a European version, not an independent witness, and none of those renderings should carry doctrinal weight without the manuscript case being made, not merely footnoted to a website. Third, the MEAT renderings of Proverbs 31 consistently select, from each word's range, whichever sense serves the moon: pelekh the distaff becomes 'the circuit,' halal becomes 'shine' three times, 'scarlet' becomes 'years,' 'time to come' becomes 'the last day.' Each choice is individually defensible; the pattern of always choosing lunar senses is a method problem, since twenty-two stacked possibilities do not equal one demonstration. Fourth, several proof-texts cut against the grain of their contexts: Job 31:26, cited to show yaqar means the moon's brightness, is Job denying that he was enticed to venerate 'the moon walking in brightness' — Scripture's one explicit warning against exactly the reverent gaze these chapters cultivate — and Deuteronomy 4:19, cited for the lights 'divided unto all nations,' is likewise a warning against being driven to worship them. Fifth, the biggest leap is calendrical: Psalm 81:3 is read so that the new-moon trumpet and the keseh fall on one day, against the natural Hebrew parallelism (trumpet at the new moon in Tishri, feast at the full moon two weeks later) and against nearly every translation; Ezekiel 46:1 plainly opens the east gate 'in the day of the new moon,' yet the chapter converts this into the full moon entering the east gate at nightfall, and then presses John 10:1 — a saying about false shepherds — into condemning the western crescent as a thief. The keseh/kisse letter-play in Proverbs 7:20 is a known variant spelling, not a revealed identity of throne and full moon. Finally, reading Matthew 7:6 so that the trampled pearls are the appointed times handed to Gentiles is homiletically clever but exegetically unanchored; the context is discretion in giving holy teaching to the unreceptive.", "paragraph_3": "Bottom line: partly persuaded, with a clear line between what is established and what is not. I am substantially persuaded that the merchant of Matthew 13:45-46 is the Son and the pearl His purchased bride — the adjacent-parable argument from Jesus's own interpretation of the sower and the field is strong, it harmonizes with Acts 20:28 and Ephesians 5:25-27, and it relieves a real tension in the traditional sinner-buys-the-kingdom reading. I am also persuaded that Scripture uses lunar reflection as a live figure for the faithful witness — Psalm 89:36-37 genuinely does set David's throne 'as the sun' and 'as the moon, a faithful witness,' Revelation 1:5 genuinely hands that title to Christ, and the Proverbs 31 woman's night vigil, borrowed shining, and appointed portions do form a suggestive constellation that the Song's 'fair as the moon' caps nicely. What the combined chapters establish, then, is a defensible symbolic reading: pearl as the one complete bride, moon as the emblem of derived, faithful light. What they do not establish is the specific identification the chapters actually want — the pearl as the full moon in an argument that terminates in a revised calendar where the full moon heads the month. That conclusion rides on the weakest links: the peninim gloss against Lamentations 4:7's redness, the collapsed reading of Psalm 81:3, the inversion of Ezekiel 46:1's new-moon gate, the keseh/kisse spelling, and an unvetted late Hebrew New Testament. The author half-concedes this in closing — 'the chain that joins the links is a reading... offered to be tested' — and I take that invitation seriously. What needs revision is a candid separation of the two theses: the symbolic case (pearl-bride-moon as figure) can stand on canonical texts and deserves a hearing even from readers formed by the traditional interpretation; the calendrical case needs independent lexical work on peninim, a real text-critical defense of the Cochin manuscripts, and an honest reckoning with Psalm 81:3 and Ezekiel 46:1 read in their own grain. Until then, I will keep the portrait and hold the calendar at arm's length — remembering, with Job, that admiring the moon's brightness must never shade into following it against the plain word of the texts that hung it there."}
